title: Ephemeral instruction sentinel design notes
content:
Goal:
- Capture a lightweight design for an 'ephemeral instruction sentinel' (EIS): a small runtime component that watches instruction sequences and applies transient policy/overrides (priority bump, prefetch hints, kill-switch) at the per-request or per-session granularity without requiring a full deploy of routing policies.

Motivation / problem statement:
- Many customers want immediate, short-lived overrides for a class of instructions (e.g., embargoed document QA, higher-fidelity inference for a VIP user experiment, or emergency safety throttle).
- Current solution requires configuration rollouts or new routing rules which are slow and heavyweight. Need a low-friction in-band signal that the serving layer can evaluate fast, audit, and fall back gracefully.

Principles:
- Minimal surface area: small JSON config attached to request or session metadata.
- Non-privileged by default: EIS cannot bypass tenant-level quotas; it only suggests routing/behavior to serving runtime which enforces safety and limits.
- Ephemeral TTL: by default short-living (seconds-minutes) and must specify expiry.
- Observability-first: every EIS decision must be traceable and produce a span / event.

High-level flow (ASCII diagram):

 client                       ingress                    routing layer                    model pool
   |                            |                            |                              |
   |---request + EIS token----->| validate EIS --+           |                              |
   |                            |                | evaluate EIS policy                  |
   |                            |                +--> maybe bump priority / route to variant
   |                            |                            |---> model instance (quantized/v2)
   |                            |                            |                              |

Notes: ingress should verify EIS signature (if any) and transform into internal "sentinel-context" proto for routing. If verification fails, drop EIS and continue with normal request path and record a metric.

EIS payload sketch (compact):
- represented as a JSON object (small keys), example below (note: this is illustrative, final should be proto):

  {
    "id": "eis-20260308-9f2b",
    "issued_by": "experiments/ui/cli",
    "target": {"tenant": "acme", "route": "chat.v1"},
    "ttl_s": 120,
    "priority": "elevate:2",            // relative bump, can be "noop" / "elevate:n" / "deprioritize:n"
    "prefetch_hint": ["embed:/user/123/last-ctx","kv:/prefill/faq-42"],
    "fallback_policy": "allow-on-quota-failover",
    "safety_level": "strict",           // hint for inline safety checks
    "signature": "base64(...)"
  }

Key fields explained:
- id: unique ephemeral id for auditing.
- issued_by: UI/CLI/service that created the EIS (string path). Could be 'admin-console' or 'canary-agent'.
- target: optional scoping. If omitted, EIS applies to the request/session by default.
- ttl_s: enforced maximum lifetime; ingress checks expiry timestamp too.
- priority: small DSL for relative queue bumping. Should map to admission control weight multiplier e.g., weight = base_weight * (1 + n*0.25).
- prefetch_hint: list of small URIs used by runtime prefetcher (embedding keys, kv keys, prompt templates). It is a hint only; runtime may ignore based on load.
- fallback_policy: what to do when request can't satisfy EIS (quota, no variant capacity). Options: drop_eis, allow_on_quota_failover, degrade_response, route_to_hosted.
- safety_level: informs additional inline checks (e.g., vetted instruction whitelist).
- signature: optional if creation endpoint signs EIS; ingress verifies using pubkey. Not required for internal quick experiments but recommended for cross-service issuance.

Ingress validation rules (sketch):
- Verify ttl_s and issued_at (if present) not expired.
- Verify signature if issued_by requires auth.
- Ensure target tenant matches request tenant.
- Limit payload size to 1KB.
- Emit metric: eis.received, eis.invalid_signature, eis.expired, eis.applied, eis.ignored.

Routing/runtime interpretation (sketch):
- Convert priority -> queue weight and admission hint.
- Prefetch hints -> prefetch queue (subject to backpressure). Prefetch items should be deduplicated per session.
- Safety_level -> invoke extra model-level filters (token or instruction sanitizer).
- If fallback_policy==degrade_response and no capacity, trigger a lightweight reranking fallback (shorter context) before returning degrade response.

Open questions / tradeoffs (brain-dump):
- Auth model: who can issue EIS? open to service accounts, admin UI, or ephemeral test tokens. Need RBAC.
- Audit: store EIS payloads in a short retention audit log and explode into long-term events if used by a revenue-impacting path.
- Signed vs unsigned: unsigned EIS great for local dev; signed recommended in prod. But signature adds verification overhead. Maybe optional but flagged in telemetry.
- Abuse surface: could repeatedly bump priorities causing starvation. Mitigation: admission control must rate-limit the total weight uplift per tenant and globally.
- Cost: elevated priority -> more preemptions and potential cost. Chargeable? For Dedicated customers, we may map to reserved capacity features.
- Complexity: runtime has to be robust to many EIS arriving concurrently; keep rule engine tiny.

Example use-cases:
- emergency throttle: create EIS with priority=deprioritize:5 for a tenant route to reduce load during upstream outage.
- VIP fast-path: issue EIS with priority=elevate:3 + prefetch_hint to warm KV and embeddings for a VIP session.
- A/B experiment: client attaches EIS with issued_by=test-harness; routing layer routes to quantized-v2 variant for a few minutes.

Telemetry/Tracing:
- Every EIS application should add a span tag: eis.id / eis.issued_by / eis.priority / eis.outcome.
- Counters: eis_applied_total, eis_ignored_total, eis_failed_validation_total.
- Histogram: eis_latency_ms (time spent evaluating and acting on EIS).

Prototype checklist for next sprint:
- [ ] Minimal proto + JSON roundtrip and size limits.
- [ ] Ingress validation and metric emission.
- [ ] Admission control mapping for priority DSL.
- [ ] Prefetch queue hook + dedupe.
- [ ] Safety hint plumbing to sanitizer service.
- [ ] End-to-end tracing (ingress -> routing -> model) with eis.* tags.
- [ ] Small hack: CLI tool to issue EIS for manual testing.

Notes to self / TODOs:
- Follow up with @Priya for RBAC matrix; ask whether product wants billing hook. (Slack: #experiments-runbooks)
- Add a short Confluence explainer and attach an example signed EIS.
- Talk to SRE about limits on prefetch queue growth.

Quick prototype API example (ingress validation endpoint) - pseudo-openapi fragment:

  POST /internal/eis/validate  -> 200 {applied: bool, reason: "ok" | "invalid_signature" | "quota_exceeded"}
  headers: X-Request-ID, X-Tenant-ID
  body: {"eis": <base64-or-json>}

Implementation constraints:
- Keep runtime changes outside core hot path: interpret EIS in a fast, precompiled switch in routing layer (avoid Lua-like slow eval).
- Keep evaluation idempotent and free of blocking network calls; prefetch can be async.

End.

(this is a rough personal scratchpad — lots of 'maybe' and TODOs; move to shared doc if we decide to push forward)
